items.example_en: The whole family was there.
items.note: 家 alone means home or family as an institution.

items.example_en: My parents live in the countryside.
items.note: Formal compound. Spoken: 爸爸妈妈.

items.example_en: My older brother is three years older than me.
items.note: 弟弟 is younger brother. Chinese never says just brother.

items.example_en: My younger sister is at university.
items.note: 姐姐 is older sister.

items.example: 他们的儿子开始上学了。
items.example_en: Their son has started school.
items.note: 女儿 is daughter. 孩子 is child.

items.example: 星期天我们去爷爷奶奶家。
items.example_en: On Sunday we're going to my grandparents'.
items.note: Maternal grandparents are 外公外婆: the two sides have separate words.

items.example_en: My husband cooks better than I do.
items.note: 老婆 is wife. Formally: 丈夫 and 妻子.

items.example_en: I'm going out with my boyfriend tonight.
items.note: 女朋友 is girlfriend. 男的朋友 with 的 means a male friend.

items.example_en: He's been single for a year.
items.note: No 是 needed; it behaves like an adjective.

items.example_en: They've been married for ten years.
items.note: A verb-object compound: you cannot say 结婚他.

items.example_en: He's a good friend of our family.
I get along really well with my older sister.
items.note: 得 links a verb to how well it is done.

items.example_en: She's tall and slim.
items.note: Adjectives need no 是, but usually take 很 as a neutral filler.

items.example_en: His hair is short and black.
items.note: 又 ... 又 ... links two qualities: both ... and ...

items.example_en: She has big eyes.
items.note: 眼镜 (yǎnjìng) means glasses: same sounds, different tone and character.

items.example_en: My colleague wears round glasses.
items.note: 戴 for accessories, 穿 for clothes and shoes.

items.example_en: You look tired.
items.note: A directional complement used figuratively.

items.example_en: She looks a lot like her father.
items.note: 长 here is zhǎng (to grow), not cháng (long).

items.example_en: The neighbours are very friendly to us.
items.note: 对 marks who the attitude is directed at.

items.example_en: Your older brother is very funny.
items.note: A phonetic loan from English humour.

items.example: 这是一个很努力的团队。
items.example_en: This is a very hard-working team.
items.note: 的 links an adjective to the noun it modifies.

items.example_en: He's a very stubborn person.
items.note: 这个人 after the subject adds a slightly critical flavour.

items.example_en: She's in a good mood today.
items.note: 心情不好 is the opposite.

items.example: 虽然很忙，她脾气还是很好。
items.example_en: Even though she's busy, she stays even-tempered.
items.note: 脾气 is temper; 发脾气 means to lose your temper.

items.example_en: I'm very happy to see you.
items.note: 开心 is the more casual equivalent.

items.example: 听到这个消息我很难过。
items.example_en: I'm very sad to hear this news.
items.note: Literally hard to pass through.

items.example_en: I'm tired, I'm going to sleep.
items.note: 了 at the end signals a change or an imminent one.

items.example_en: I'm afraid of flying.
items.note: A verb, so it needs no 很 and no 是.

items.example_en: I can't stand this noise.
items.note: A potential complement. The positive is 受得了.

items.example_en: Work has been very stressful lately.
items.note: Literally the pressure is big.

items.example_en: He quit? Really?
You passed? That's great!
items.note: 太 ... 了 is a fixed frame for exclamations.

items.example_en: Luckily it didn't rain.
items.note: Also answers 你好吗 with a mild fine.

items.example_en: Are you coming? It depends.
items.note: Literally look at the situation.

items.example_en: I'm fine, and you?
items.note: 呢 bounces a question back without repeating it.

items.example_en: Anyway, we had a great time.
items.note: Wraps up a rambling story.
